title: Taniyan (Kureśar)
sanskrit: श्रीवत्सचिह्नमिश्रेभ्यो नमः उक्ति मदधीमहे। यदुक्तयास्त्रयीकण्ठे यान्ति मङ्गलसूत्रताम्॥
transliteration: śrīvatsacihna-miśrebhyo namaḥ ukti-madhīmahe | yad uktayāḥ trayī-kaṇṭhe yānti maṅgala-sūtratām ||
translation: Salutations to Sri Srivatsachihna Mishra whose utterances have become the auspicious thread adorning the neck of Veda Mata.
commentary:
This verse is traditionally recited before commencing the Sri Sthavam. It is a salutation to Kūreśa, also known as Srivatsachihna Mishra, the revered disciple of Bhagavad Rāmānuja and the composer of the Sri Sthavam. By likening his sacred utterances to the maṅgala-sūtra adorning the Veda Mata, the taniyan underscores the auspicious and authoritative nature of his words.

The 'trayī' refers to the three Vedas (Rig, Yajur, Sāma), which are metaphorically personified as a bride. The utterances of Kūreśa are so revered and pure that they are considered fit to be the ornament around the neck of this divine bride. The sentiment here is one of deep respect, recognizing the inseparability of his teachings from the Vedic tradition.

In Śrī Vaiṣṇava sampradāya, a taniyan serves not only to honor the author but also to prepare the devotee's mind, aligning it with the spirit of the work to be recited. Thus, beginning with this salutation invokes both reverence and receptivity in the seeker.

sanskrit: स्वस्ति श्रीर्दिशतादशेषजगतां सर्गोपसर्गस्थितिः स्वर्गं दुर्गतिमापवर्गिकपदं सर्वं च कुर्वन् हरिः। यस्या वीक्ष्यमुखं तदिङ्गितपराधीनो विधत्तेऽखिलं क्रीडेयं खलु नान्यथाऽस्य रसदा स्यादैक‌रस्यात्तया॥
transliteration: svasti śrīr diśatād aśeṣa–jagatāṃ sargopasarga–sthitiḥ svargaṃ durgatim āpavargika–padaṃ sarvaṃ ca kurvan hariḥ | yasyā vīkṣya mukhaṃ tadingita–parādhīno vidhatte 'khilaṃ krīḍeyaṃ khalu nānyathā'sya rasadā syād aikarasyāt tayā ||
translation: May Sri Devi, whose auspicious face guides Lord Hari in creation, dissolution, and protection — making Him act according to Her slightest wish — bless all worlds with well-being.
commentary:
In this opening verse, Kureśa invokes blessings upon all the worlds by seeking the grace of Śrī, the divine consort of Lord Hari. The phrase 'svasti śrīr diśatād' serves as a benediction: may auspicious Śrī confer well-being.

Hari is described as the one who carries out the acts of creation (sarga), protection (sthiti), and dissolution (upasarga), as well as granting svarga (heavenly pleasures), durgati (release from suffering), and āpavarga (final liberation). Yet, for all His independence and supreme power, He remains attentive to the slightest indication (tad-iṅgita-parādhīnaḥ) from Her countenance before acting.

This relationship is one of perfect unity and harmony, which the poet calls 'aikarasyam' — an undivided oneness of will and joy. Without this companionship, the play of creation and protection would lose its rasa (delight) for Him.

The verse reflects a central theme in Śrī Vaiṣṇava philosophy: the inseparable association of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa in all divine functions. Swāmi Deśikan’s works, such as the Śrī Stuti, echo this sentiment: 'viṣṇus tvam ca iti dvandvam anyonyalakṣyam'.

By drawing attention to this divine unity, the poet teaches that the devotee must always approach the Lord through Her, for it is Her glance and consent that sweeten and sanctify His cosmic play.

sanskrit: हे श्रीर्देवि! समस्तलोकजननीं त्वां स्तोतुमीहमहे युक्तां भावय भारतीं प्रगुणया प्रेमप्रधानां धियम्। भक्तिं बन्धय नन्दयाश्रितमिमं दासं जनं तावकं, लक्ष्म्यं लक्ष्मि! कदाक्षवेचिविसृतेः ते स्याम चामे वयम्॥
transliteration: he śrīr devi! samasta–loka–jananīṃ tvāṃ stotum īhamahe yuktāṃ bhāvaya bhāratīṃ praguṇayā prema–pradhānāṃ dhiyam | bhaktiṃ bandhaya nandayāśritam imaṃ dāsaṃ janaṃ tāvakam, lakṣmyaṃ lakṣmi! kadākṣa–veci–visṛteḥ te syāma cāme vayam ||
translation: O Mother of the worlds, Maha Lakshmi! I aspire to praise You. Bless me with fitting speech, a mind rich in love, and devotion to serve You.
commentary:
Kurēśa directly addresses Śrī as 'samasta–loka–jananī' — the mother of all worlds — and expresses his intent to praise Her. He petitions Her to inspire in him a fitting Bhāratī (speech) imbued with praguṇa (excellence) and prema–pradhāna (predominance of love) so that the hymn he composes is worthy.

He also prays for bhakti (devotion) to be firmly bound within him (bhaktiṃ bandhaya) and for joy (nandaya) in the servitude he renders (āśritam imaṃ dāsaṃ). This servitude is total — he identifies himself as 'tāvakā' (belonging to You).

Finally, his plea extends beyond himself — 'syāma cāme vayam' — may I and these others (fellow devotees) all become recipients of the 'kadākṣa–veci–visṛti' — the outpouring wave of Her merciful sidelong glance.

The verse teaches that the devotee should seek three essentials from the Goddess before undertaking service: pure speech, a love-filled mind, and steadfast devotion, all validated by Her grace-laden glance.

sanskrit: स्तोत्रं नाम किमामनन्ति कवयो यद्यन्यधीयान् गुणान् अन्यत्र त्वसतोऽधिरोप्य फणितिः सा तर्हि वन्ध्या त्वयि। सम्यक् सत्यम् गुणाभिवर्णनमतो ब्रूयुः कथं तादृशी वाग्वाचस्पतिना ऽपि शक्यरचना त्वत्सद्गुणार्णोनिधौ॥
transliteration: stotraṃ nāma kim āmananti kavayo yady anyadhīyān guṇān anyatra tv asato 'dhiropya phaṇitiḥ sā tarhi vandhyā tvayi | samyak satya–guṇābhivarṇanam atho brūyuḥ kathaṃ tādṛśī vāg vācaspati–nā 'pi śakya–racanā tvat–sad–guṇārṇo–nidhau ||
translation: Poets often praise non-existent or limited qualities in others, but with You there is neither exaggeration nor deficiency — Your virtues are infinite.
commentary:
Kurēśa reflects on the nature of poetic praise. In the world, poets tend to embellish — yady anyadhīyān guṇān anyatra tv-asataḥ — borrowing imagined virtues from elsewhere and attaching them to their subject, making their praise empty ('vandhyā').

In the case of Śrī, however, no such exaggeration is possible or necessary. Her sattva–guṇas (true auspicious attributes) are limitless ('tvat–sad–guṇārṇo–nidhau' — in the ocean–treasure of Your good qualities). Therefore, describing Her accurately (samyak–satya–guṇābhivarṇanam) is itself the stotra.

Even Vācaspati (Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods) would find it impossible to compose (śakya–racanā) poetry that fully encapsulates these immeasurable qualities. This underscores the humility of the poet and the immeasurable greatness of the Goddess.

sanskrit: ये वाचां मनसां च दुर्ग्रहतया ख्याताः गुणास्तावकाः तानेव प्रति साम्बुजिह्वमुदिता हे मामिका भारती। हास्यं तत्तु न मन्यहे न हि चकोरैकाखिलां चन्द्रिकां नालं पातुमिति प्रगृह्य रसनाऽसीत सत्यान् तृषि॥
transliteration: ye vācāṃ manasāṃ ca durgrahatayā khyātāḥ guṇās tāvakāḥ tān eva prati sāmbujihvāmuditā he māmikā bhāratī | hāsyaṃ tat tu na manyahe na hi cakoryaikākhilāṃ candrikāṃ nālaṃ pātum iti pragṛhya rasanā āsīt satyāṃ tṛṣi ||
translation: Your glories are impossible to grasp with mind or speech. My attempt is like the chakora bird trying to drink all the moonlight.
commentary:
Here Kurēśa notes that Śrī's attributes are known to be beyond capture by word ('vācām') and mind ('manasām'). Yet, Bhāratī (Vāk Devī, Goddess of Speech) herself delights ('amuditā') in turning towards them.

The speaker likens his attempt to praise Her to a chakora bird which craves moonlight: it is not considered laughable ('hāsyaṃ') even if it cannot drink the entire ('ekākhilāṃ') flood of lunar rays ('candrikām'). The effort itself is an expression of love and longing.

Admitting his inability does not dissuade the poet — instead he frames his work as a joyful act of devotion, relishing the very thirst (satyaṃ tṛṣi) that spurs praise.

sanskrit: क्षोदीयानपि दुष्टबुद्धिरपि निस्स्नेहोऽप्यनीहोऽपि ते कीर्तिं देवि लिहन्महम् न च बिभेम्यज्ञो न जिघृणेमि च। दुःश्येत सा तु न तावता न हि शुना लीडाऽपि भागीरथी दुःश्येच्छ्वापि न लज्जते न च बिभेत्यार्तिः तु साम्येच्छुनः॥
transliteration: kṣodīyān api duṣṭa-buddhir api nissneho 'py anīho 'pi te kīrtiṃ devi lihann aham na ca bibhemy ajño na jigṛṇemi ca | duḥśyeta sā tu na tāvatā na hi śunā līḍā 'pi bhāgīrathī duḥśyecc hvāpi na lajjate na ca bibhety ārtiḥ tu sāmye cchunaḥ ||
translation: Though unworthy, I am unashamed to praise You. Like a dog drinking from the Ganga, I cannot pollute Your sanctity.
commentary:
Kurēśa humbles himself thoroughly, calling his own mind 'duṣṭa-buddhi' (corrupt) and lacking affection ('nissneha') and initiative ('anīha').

Yet he proceeds to 'lick' (lihan) at the Goddess’s glory, without fear ('na ca bibhemi') or shame ('na jighṛṇemi').

To illustrate, he offers the analogy of a dog ('śunā') drinking from the sacred Gaṅgā. The river is not polluted ('duḥśyeta') by the dog’s contact, and the dog is certainly not shamed or afraid. The river remains pure regardless of the drinker’s impurity.

Similarly, Lakṣmī's sanctity remains unaffected by the poet's shortcomings; instead, in the very act of approaching Her, he is cleansed and his thirst for grace is quenched.

sanskrit: ऐश्वर्यं महदेव वाल्पमथवा दृश्येत पुंसां हि यत्तल्लक्ष्म्याः समुदीक्षणात् तव यतः सार्वत्रिकं वर्तते। तेनैतेन न विस्मयेमहि जगन्नाथोऽपि नारायणः धन्यं मन्यते ईक्षणात् तव यतः स्वात्मानमात्मेश्वरः॥
transliteration: aiśvaryaṃ mahad eva vālpam athavā dṛśyeta puṃsāṃ hi yat tallakṣmyāḥ samudīkṣaṇāt tava yataḥ sārvatrikaṃ vartate | tena etena na vismayemahi jagannātho 'pi nārāyaṇaḥ dhanyaṃ manyate īkṣaṇāt tava yataḥ svātmānam ātmeśvaraḥ ||
translation: All forms of wealth, great or small, come from Your merciful glance. Even Narayana counts Himself blessed when Your gaze falls upon Him.
commentary:
Here, Kurēśa extols the Goddess’s 'samudīkṣaṇa' — Her all-encompassing, compassionate gaze — as the source of all 'aiśvarya' (prosperity, sovereignty). Whether a being has great or small fortune, it is owed solely to that glance.

He points out that even Nārāyaṇa, the 'Ātmeśvara' (Lord of Himself), the 'Jagannātha' (Lord of the Universe), considers Himself blessed ('dhanyaṃ manyate') when graced by Her vision.

Thus the devotee should not be surprised ('na vismayemahi') that all prosperity flows through Her — even the Supreme Lord basks in the privilege of Her attention.

sanskrit: ऐश्वर्यं यदशेष पुंसि यदिदं सौनन्दर्यलावण्ययोः रूपं यच्च हि मङ्गलं किमपि यल्लोके सिद्ध्युच्यते। तत्सर्वं त्वद्धीनमेव यततः श्रीरित्यभेदेन वा यद्वा श्रीमदितीदृशेन वचसा देवि प्रथमस्नुते॥
transliteration: aiśvaryaṃ yadaśeṣa puṃsi yad idaṃ saundarya-lāvaṇyayoḥ rūpaṃ yac ca hi maṅgalaṃ kim api yat loke siddhy ucyate | tat sarvaṃ tvad-dhīnam eva yataḥ śrīr ity abhedena vā yad vā śrī-mat iti īdṛśena vacasā devi pratham asnute ||
translation: Whatever wealth, beauty, or auspiciousness beings possess is Yours. All derive from their connection to You.
commentary:
The poet generalises the theme of the previous verse: every form of 'aiśvarya' (prosperity), 'rūpa' (form), 'saundarya-lāvaṇya' (beauty and grace), and 'maṅgala' (auspiciousness) found anywhere in creation belongs to Śrī.

Some entities are directly identified with Her, as in calling them 'Śrī' itself (śrīr iti abhedena), while others are acknowledged as being endowed with Her ('śrīmat') — but in both cases the underlying truth is that their qualities stem from Her ownership and association.

By highlighting this, the poet shows that all worldly and spiritual excellences ultimately trace back to the Goddess.

sanskrit: देवि त्वन्महिमावधिर्न हरिणा नापि त्वया ज्ञायते यद्यप्येवमथापि नैव युभयोः सर्वज्ञता हीयते। यन्नास्त्येव तदज्ञानमनुगुणं सर्वज्ञतायाः विदुः व्योमाम्भोजमिदन्तया किल विदन्भ्रान्तोऽयमित्युच्यते॥
transliteration: devi tvan–mahimāvadhiḥ na hariṇā nāpi tvayā jñāyate yady apy evam athāpi naiva yuvayoḥ sarvajñatā hīyate | yan nāsty eva tad ajñānam anuguṇaṃ sarvajñatāyā viduḥ vyoma–ambhojam idantayā kila vidan bhrānto 'yam ity ucyate ||
translation: Neither You nor even Hari know the limit of Your greatness, for such a limit does not exist. Ignorance of a non-existent boundary is not a flaw in omniscience.
commentary:
Kurēśa proclaims that the 'mahimā–avadhi' (limit of greatness) of the Goddess is unknown not only to others but also to Nārāyaṇa Himself — and even to Her. This is not due to any lack of omniscience, but because such a limit simply does not exist.

He explains: ignorance pertains only to an existing thing whose nature is unknown. When something does not exist at all (like a 'sky–lotus', vyoma–ambhoja), not knowing it is in fact knowledge of its non–existence. Thus, the absence of knowledge of a non–existent limit does not diminish the all–knowing nature ('sarvajñatā') of either.

The analogy to the mythical sky–lotus helps the listener grasp that Her glories are boundless and inexpressible.

sanskrit: लोके वनस्पति-बृहस्पति-तारतम्यं यस्याः प्रसाद-परिणामम् उदाहरन्ति। सा भारती भगवती तु यदीया दासी तां देव-देव-महिषीं श्रियमाश्रयामः॥
transliteration: loke vanaspati–bṛhaspati–tāratamyaṃ yasyāḥ prasāda–pariṇāmam udāharanti | sā bhāratī bhagavatī tu yadīyā dāsī tāṃ deva–deva–mahiṣīṃ śriyam āśrayāmaḥ ||
translation: The hierarchy of trees and of scholars is due to Saraswati’s grace, and Saraswati herself is Your maidservant. I take refuge in You, the Queen of the Lord of Lords.
commentary:
Two analogies are given: vanaspati–tāratamya (the hierarchy among trees) and bṛhaspati–tāratamya (hierarchy among scholars). These differences in excellence are due to the 'prasāda–pariṇāma' — the transformative grace — of the Goddess.

Astonishingly, even Bhāratī (Sarasvatī), the goddess of learning and speech, is described here as a servant ('dāsī') of Śrī. Thus all speech, wisdom, and learning ultimately serve Her.

Concluding the verse, the poet declares his own surrender to Her — 'śriyam āśrayāmaḥ' — identifying Her as the 'deva–deva–mahiṣī', queen of the Supreme Lord.

sanskrit: यस्याः कटाक्ष-मृदु-वीक्षण-दीक्षणेन सद्यः समुल्लसित-पल्लवम् उल्ललास। विश्वं विपर्यय-समुत्थ-विपर्ययं प्राक् तां देव-देव-महिषीं श्रियमाश्रयामः॥
transliteration: yasyāḥ kaṭākṣa–mṛdu–vīkṣaṇa–dīkṣaṇena sadyaḥ samullasita–pallavam ullalāsa | viśvaṃ viparyaya–samuttha–viparyayaṃ prāk tāṃ deva–deva–mahiṣīṃ śriyam āśrayāmaḥ ||
translation: Before Your gracious glance, the world lay dormant after the cosmic dissolution. The very intention to look revived it.
commentary:
Kurēśa describes the tender ('mṛdu') glance ('vīkṣaṇa') of Śrī as life–giving. At the time of creation, the universe lay in a state of inactivity and inversion ('viparyaya–samuttha–viparyayaṃ'), much like sproutless seeds after dissolution.

By the mere resolve of the Goddess to cast Her compassionate glance, the 'pallava' (fresh shoots) of creation sprang forth ('samullasita–pallavam'). This reanimation of the cosmos underscores Her role not only as the consort of the Lord but as an active principle in creation.

The poet again affirms his surrender, seeking refuge in the 'deva–deva–mahiṣī', the empress of the Lord of Lords.

sanskrit: यस्याः कटाक्ष-वीक्षा-क्षण-लक्षणं लक्षिता महेशा: स्युः। श्रीरङ्ग-राज-महिषी सा मामपि वीक्षतां लक्ष्मीः॥
transliteration: yasyāḥ kaṭākṣa–vīkṣā–kṣaṇa–lakṣaṇaṃ lakṣitā maheśāḥ syuḥ | śrī–raṅga–rāja–mahiṣī sā mām api vīkṣatāṃ lakṣmīḥ ||
translation: A mere moment of Your glance grants the greatest wealth. O Queen of Sriranga, Lakshmi! Cast Your eyes upon me as well.
commentary:
The final śloka distills the prayer into the simplest, most heartfelt wish: that the Goddess may glance upon the poet. The illustrious 'maheśāḥ' — great lords — become blessed by a mere moment’s ('kṣaṇa') worth of Her 'kaṭākṣa–vīkṣā' (sidelong glance).

Kurēśa identifies Her here as the 'Śrīraṅga–rāja–mahiṣī', the Queen of Lord Ranganātha in Śrīraṅgam. The implicit teaching is that if even the greatest are ennobled by Her glance, then so too will the humble devotee be infinitely benefited by it.

By ending with this plea, the hymn comes full circle — from describing Her cosmic role in verse 1 to seeking personal grace in verse 11 — reinforcing that the ultimate goal is to secure Her merciful sight.

title: Dhyāna Śloka
sanskrit: कल्याणानामविकलनिधिः कापि कारुण्यसीमा नित्यामोदा निगमवचसां मौलिमन्दारमाला। संपद्दिव्या मधुविजयिनः सन्निधत्तां सदा मे सैषा देवी सकलभुवनप्रार्थना कामधेनुः॥
transliteration: kalyāṇānām avikala–nidhiḥ kāpi kāruṇya–sīmā nityāmudā nigama–vacasām mauli–mandāra–mālā | sampad divyā madhu–vijayinaḥ sannidhattāṃ sadā me saiṣā devī sakala–bhuvana–prārthanā kāma–dhenuḥ ||
translation: She is the inexhaustible treasure of auspiciousness, the very boundary of mercy, the eternal delight and garland on the Vedas’ head; the supreme wealth of Lord Vishnu, the wish-yielding cow for all worlds. May such Devi always reside in my heart.
commentary:
This dhyāna–śloka serves as a meditative closing, encapsulating the essence of the entire stava. Śrī is described as the 'avikala–nidhiḥ' (unfailing treasure) of all kalyāṇas (auspicious qualities) and the ultimate boundary or measure of compassion (kāruṇya–sīmā).

She is 'nityāmudā' — ever-blissful — and termed the 'mauli–mandāra–mālā', meaning the garland of coral-tree flowers adorning the head (mauli) of the Vedas themselves ('nigama–vacasām').

She is the 'sampad divyā' (divine wealth) of 'madhu–vijayin' (the conqueror of Madhu, i.e., Mahā Viṣṇu), and the 'kāma–dhenuḥ' (wish-fulfilling cow) to whom all the worlds address their highest prayers and desires.

By meditating on Her in this form, the devotee aspires for Her constant presence ('sannidhattām sadā me') in his heart, ensuring that both his spiritual and worldly needs are forever met.
